subjects.displayTitle: The Letters of the Living: recognition and responsibility
subjects.introduction: Eighteen souls, the Báb said, must find Him unwarned and uninvited, each searching alone and recognizing His Revelation of their own accord, before His pilgrimage could begin. The Letters of the Living are first of all a story about recognition without the comfort of a crowd. Yet the honour of being first was only an entrance: those same men scattered across Persia to carry the message, one of them accompanied the Báb to Mecca, and the rest of each life had still to be lived, faithfully or otherwise. Jesus sending out the twelve to announce the kingdom and give freely what they had freely received offers a parallel movement from calling to service [1]. The Báb counts the Letters with Himself as nineteen, a number that shapes the Bahá’í month and feast, and He describes them as letters of a word and mirrors facing a sun, images of participation in a light that is not their own and that withdraws when the mirror turns away. The journey continues toward Quddús and Ṭáhirih, the most luminous of the Letters, and toward the station and claims of the Báb.
subjects.arc: Begin with independent recognition, follow the movement into service, and then examine how honor, symbolic station, and enduring faithfulness relate to one another.

order.why: Open with the challenge of recognizing a revelation independently.
Follow the early believers outward into the work of spreading the message.
shortened: Of this number Mulla Husayn of Bushruyih, Mirza Ahmad of Azghand, Mulla Sadiq Muqaddas [the Holy], Shaykh Abu-Turab of Ishtihard, Mulla Yusuf of Ardibil, Mulla Jalil of Urumiyyih, Mulla Mihdi of Kand, Shaykh Sa'id the Indian, Mulla 'Ali of Bastam, and the like of these came out unto Him and spread themselves through all parts of Persia.

order.why: Hear the distinction bestowed upon one of the Letters.
Explore the gratitude expressed for the first believer’s role in guidance.
Read the Letters within the Báb’s language of divine friendship and command.
shortened: And proclaim from My true tongue that "Verily I am God, there is no God but I. I have created all things by My command, and verily Muhammad is My servant and My Messenger, and verily the Letters of the Living are My friends, and likewise the Twin Gates are My doors, for verily I am God, there is no God but I. I have created the heavens and earth by My command more swiftly than uttering the word 'Be.'"

order.why: Identifies the first and last Letters of the Living and clarifies that Mirza Yahya was not among them.
Pause over a prayer for the martyrs and the Letters.
shortened: Therefore, O God, do Thou send down upon him and upon the Letters of the Living and upon all his names and likenesses that which befitteth the loftiness of Thy sanctity and the exaltation of Thy grace.

order.why: Introduce the symbolic reckoning of the first circle and further holy souls.
shortened: In this wondrous cycle there are the eighteen Letters of the Living and the sacred person of the Exalted One, which total nineteen persons, and likewise five other holy and blessed souls whose mention wisdom does not now permit - it will later become manifest and apparent.

order.why: Compare the formulation of nineteen including the Primal Point.
Preserve the acknowledgment that five identities remain unknown.
shortened: Regarding the twenty-four chosen ones mentioned in the Holy Book and discussed in 'Abdu'l-Baha's Some Answered Questions - nineteen of them were the Point of Truth and Letters of the Living who have passed away. The other five remain unknown until now.

order.why: Keep the numerical statement that calls for reading its larger explanation.
Connect the number to the reported explanation of nineteen days.
shortened: 1st question: - What is the real meaning of the 19 days feast, spiritual and material?
Answer: "Nineteen days are according to 19 'Letters of the Living' which is composed of the Bab and 18 others.

order.why: Retain the brief record of a later encounter with Bahá’u’lláh.
shortened: One day in Baghdad, very early in the morning, Mulla Baqir, one of the Letters of the Living, attained the presence of Baha'u'llah.

order.why: Clarify the supplied identification of the first believer.
shortened: The first to believe in the Primal Point, may my spirit be sacrificed for Him, was the revered Mulla Husayn-i-Bushrui, the Babu'l-Bab, not Quddus.

order.why: Hear the Letters described through belief and the delivery of a message. Consider the relation between obedience and inward guidance.
shortened: Say: All the Messengers together, and all the angels together, and all the truthful ones together, and all the martyrs together, and all those brought nigh together, and all the believers together, and all the sincere ones together, and all the righteous ones together, and all the guided ones together, and all those who trust in God, their Lord, the All-Merciful, together, and all those who commit their affairs to God, their Lord, together, and those who recite the Book of God and are assured of it, all together - God has promised to reward them with a goodly recompense and to cause them to enter a blessed abode from His presence.

Say: There is no mercy beside the mercy of God, and all seek mercy through His mercy. Say: There are no words except the words of God; therefore efface the conditions of your own selves if ye desire to be guided.

order.why: Enter the symbolic language of names and the number of the Living.
shortened: For They consist of fourteen sacred Souls, and the Hidden, Well-Guarded Name, Whose four letters are called by various names including the Four Gates, the Lights of the Throne, and the Bearers of creation, provision, death, and life. Together They comprise the number of the word the Living (hayy=18), Who are the most near Names unto God. All others besides Them are guided through Their guidance, inasmuch as God hath proceeded the creation of the Bayan from Them, and hath ordained that unto Them they shall return.

order.why: Distinguish the honor of early belief from the subsequent course of a life.
Turn from rank to the practical call for steadfast remembrance and service.
Retain the unfinished prayerful passage without inventing its ending.
Close with the mirror image and the warning against repeating inherited barriers to recognition.
shortened: The Letters of the Unity He described---by the guidance of the Furqan---as fourteen "returns," the first four being the four Gates, and these souls He named the Letters of the Living, giving them precedence above all that are in the Bayan. After this rank He spoke of the Mirrors; and thou mayest observe that in none of His limited Tablets did He confine the Mirrors, even as He declareth that were infinite Mirrors to stand face to face, in all of them the lights of the Sun would be imprinted and made manifest; and after their turning away He saith that that grace is withdrawn. He set forth the likeness of the outward mirror and the visible sun, and declared that whoso desireth to attain unto recognition must behold the manifest Sun and the manifest Mirrors. He swept away all the limiting definitions of the Furqan, so that unto every discerning eye it became evident that in the hands of that people there was naught in support of the Truth, and whatsoever they possessed was wholly contrary thereto.

questions: What might independent recognition require when no established community yet confirms a person’s judgment?
How does the collection distinguish the honor of being first from the work of remaining faithful?
What do the images of letters and mirrors suggest about participation in a revelation?
How might the first believers’ story prepare a reader to recognize an unexpected new responsibility in their own life?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the claim about revelation that the early believers were called to recognize.
Consider the distinction between the Herald, Bahá’u’lláh, and the station of service.

references.label: 1 · Matthew 10:5–10 — receiving a message and carrying it outward
references.note: Jesus sends the twelve with a particular mission, joining proclamation to healing and a freely given service. Compare the movement from recognition to action with the Letters of the Living. The two accounts have different settings and instructions; the comparison concerns what a calling asks of those who receive it.

subjects.displayTitle: The Báb’s resting place: a trust carried through danger
subjects.introduction: Sixty years. That is how long the body of the Báb was moved from hiding place to hiding place, carried by palanquin and steamer, concealed from enemies, never allowed to rest, before it was laid on Naw-Rúz in a marble sarcophagus on the slope of Mount Carmel. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá called the undertaking at once the most difficult and the most triumphant work of the Cause, and his announcements of the interment repeat the word rest with an almost audible release of breath. The devotion involved was practical as well as tender: a martyr who carried the remains to Tehran, inspectors at customs, gold lettering ordered from Bombay, stone laid by many hands. Mark tells how Joseph of Arimathaea went to Pilate for the body of Jesus, provided linen, and laid Him in the tomb while others watched the place [1]; in both stories love after a violent death takes the form of concrete responsibility. From the Shrine the path opens onto the martyrdom that made it necessary, onto the station and claims of the Báb Himself, and onto the wider meaning of shrines and holy places as living centres of a community.
subjects.arc: Begin with the difficulty of the undertaking, attend to the people and materials that made it possible, and hear the repeated glad tidings of a resting place.

order.why: Hear the extended announcement of interment after years of danger.
shortened: O spiritual friends! The greatest glad-tidings is that the pure, luminous, and holy remains of His Holiness the Exalted One (may my spirit be sacrificed for Him), after being moved from place to place for sixty years due to the control of enemies and fear of the hostile ones, never finding rest or repose, through the grace of the Blessed Beauty was finally established, on the day of Naw-Ruz with utmost ceremony and perfect majesty and beauty, in the sacred casket at the most exalted spot on Mount Carmel.

order.why: Open with the task described as both difficult and triumphant.
Attend to the explicit direction to a particular historical account.
Follow the reverent movement of the remains toward the Holy Land.
shortened: With complete humility and reverence they brought the Most Great Throne - the pure body and sacred temple (may my spirit and being be sacrificed for His dust) - by palanquin to the land of Syria and by steamer to the Holy Land.

order.why: Notice the material preparation and obstacles at customs.
Bring the shared work of constructing the Shrine into view.
shortened: In particular, now that I am busy with the construction of the Shrine of the Bab, I had intended for you to help me in every aspect of the raising of this Sacred Edifice.

order.why: Read another announcement locating that joy on Naw-Rúz.
Attend to the imagery of light and rejoicing at the resting place.
Let the concise statement of repose gather the journey into one image.
shortened: The sacred remains of His Holiness the Exalted One, may my soul be a sacrifice for Him, after sixty years of wandering, have found repose in the holy spot of Mount Carmel, the divine garden of Carmel.

order.why: Retain the parallel testimony naming the Mountain of God.
Describes the Bab’s remains resting in the Shrine on Mount Carmel and the spiritual significance of that setting.
Hear the repeated emphasis upon rest after wandering.
shortened: For after sixty years of restlessness and wandering, the sacred remains of the Exalted One - may my spirit be sacrificed for His wrongs - found repose on Mount Carmel.

order.why: Widen remembrance to the growth of the Sanctuary’s surroundings.
Recall the steadfast delivery of a divine message under oppression.
Read the supplied report announcing safe arrival outside Iran.
shortened: The good news that I had promised is this: the sacred remains of the Exalted Bab have safely left the soil of Iran and just arrived in the Ottoman land. They are now completely out of danger. After fifty years, what the Blessed Beauty promised has come to pass. In gratitude for this most great divine blessing, lives must be sacrificed! Soon will the effulgence of the Shrine of the Bab attract the attention of the denizens of the world and the blessed prophecies of Baha'u'llah will be clearly fulfilled.

order.why: Preserve the separately supplied account of the marble sarcophagus.
Retain the excerpt announcing the appointed resting place and its internal omission.
shortened: O friends of 'Abdu'l-Baha! In these days, through divine decree, the confirmation of the Lord of the highest heavens, and the grace of the invisible Kingdom, the sacred remains of the Bab have been laid to rest in their designated place on Mount Carmel in Haifa.
The blessed body of the Martyred One has been entirely laid to rest on Mount Carmel.

order.why: Close with the separately identified account of Afnán’s burial as another expression of reverent care.

questions: How does attention to transport, materials, and practical arrangements deepen the meaning of devotion in these accounts?
What changes when repeated words about rest are read against the long period of insecurity they describe?
How can a community preserve both the reverence and the historical precision required by sacred memory?
What relationship might connect care for a resting place with the continuing life and service of a community?

neighbors.invitation: Read a prayer that places the martyrs and the Letters within a shared remembrance.
Consider another supplied account of the pressures of exile and confiscation.

references.label: 1 · Mark 15:42–47 — care for the body of Jesus
references.note: Joseph approaches Pilate, obtains the body, provides linen, and lays Jesus in a tomb while others observe the place. Compare the practical acts that carry devotion through grief and danger with the care described here. The different histories remain distinct, while both make remembrance inseparable from concrete human responsibility.

subjects.displayTitle: The Qá’im: expectation and the question of recognition
subjects.introduction: The Báb declared himself to be the Qá’im whose Day all were awaiting, and in doing so stepped into the oldest longing of Shí‘ih Islam. At once the questions came from the pulpits: what of Jábulqá and Jábulsá, the Minor and Major Occultations, the conquest of East and West, the signs recorded from the Holy Family? Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answer not by dismissing the traditions but by reading them again. The reports about the twelfth Imám are confused and contradictory, they note, and the reconciliation lies in distinguishing a reality that existed in the unseen realm from a bodily appearance on the day of manifestation. Recognition then becomes less a matching of signs than an entry into a fire that tests certitude. An explanation of the Qur’ánic verse on the descent of the angels and the Spirit identifies the Spirit with the Qá’im and the angels with the Imáms, inviting close comparison with the verse itself [1]. This is a Bábí and Bahá’í reading of the promise, not a survey of all Muslim understandings. The path leads on to the Báb himself and his claims, to the Primal Point, and to the Imamate from which the expectation grew.
subjects.arc: Begin with the declaration, encounter the questions it provoked, and then consider interpretation, spiritual reality, and the response demanded by a claim of fulfillment.

order.why: Hear the declaration through several inherited names and titles.
Open with the direct declaration of the awaited station.
shortened: Verily, I am the Qa'im Whose Day all await, and through Whom all have been promised.

order.why: Connect the claim with revealed verses and evidences.
Encounter the cluster of objections arising from expected signs.
Ask how the language of transmitted traditions is to be approached.
Notice the explicit acknowledgment of varied and conflicting reports.
Read the proposed reconciliation of spiritual existence and bodily appearance.
Names the four appointed intermediaries of the Twelfth Imam during the Lesser Occultation.
Compare the explanation distinguishing the unseen realm from a material history.
Return to the identification of the Báb with the promised One.
shortened: The Twelfth Imam, the Exalted One (may my spirit be sacrificed for Him), Who was the seal of the preceding Imams and the opener of divine favors, declared at the beginning of His manifestation and mention of the Imamate that "I am that promised One," and all the Shi'ites were awaiting the appearance of the Twelfth Imam.

order.why: Consider the station of servitude described for followers.
Approach recognition as entry into an encounter.
shortened: Whosoever entereth therein, these are they who shall thereafter know that He is the Qa'im unto Whom all supplicate night and day, and all are promised His day.

order.why: Read the fire image used for the testing of certitude.
shortened: These are they upon whom blessings are sent and who submit themselves. The example of this Cause is like the fire of God which He will manifest on the Day of Resurrection. Those who enter therein, they are the ones who attain certitude that He is the Qa'im whom those in the kingdoms of the heavens and earth and what lies between them await, and all know Him by His command.

order.why: Pause over the summons to listen to revelation.
Notice the expectation that even exalted leaders may turn away.
Retain the concise challenge to inherited reports.
Examine the dramatic distinction between the promised and the imagined.
Consider how one expectation of return can itself become a veil to another revelation.
shortened: Rather, the joy of those days relates to their belief that the Imams have returned and appeared, in accordance with Shi'ih belief, for among the authenticated traditions is that at the appearance of the Qa'im, the Imams of the Qur'an will arise from their graves and appear. They are unaware that in these days another Cause has appeared and the hidden treasure has been revealed.

order.why: End with an explicit interpretation of a Qur’ánic verse for further comparison.

questions: What kinds of evidence do these passages place beside inherited expectations about the promised figure?
How does distinguishing spiritual reality from bodily appearance change the questions a reader asks of a tradition?
What might prevent the interpretation of a promise from becoming so fixed that no encounter could challenge it?
How does comparing Qur’án 97:4 with the interpretation given here reveal the work that an interpreter is doing?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the independent recognition asked of the first believers.
Explore another distinction between an enduring spiritual station and its appearance in history.

references.label: 1 · Qur’án 97:4 — the angels and the Spirit
references.note: The verse describes the descent of the angels and the Spirit by divine permission. Compare its wording, including the differences visible among these translations, with the supplied interpretation identifying the Spirit with the Qá’im and the angels with the Imáms. Distinguish the verse itself from the specific interpretive claim made about it.

subjects.displayTitle: Bahá’u’lláh: a life seen through its light
subjects.introduction: How is a Messenger of God recognized? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá points first to what Bahá’u’lláh does in people: He frees them from the darkness of inherited prejudice, draws hostile sects toward one another, and kindles a love that crosses every border. Those who knew Him remember a presence so awe-inspiring that visitors knelt without meaning to, a face on which joy and sorrow were plainly visible, and a man who described Himself simply as unschooled and untraveled, born into the household of a government official. His very existence, one witness said, was itself a miracle. Jesus, too, asked those who questioned Him to look at His works [1], and the comparison invites an attention that weighs words and conduct together. From here the path runs back through the early years of a gifted childhood, down into the darkness of the Síyáh-Chál and the long road of exile, and on toward the Declaration in which He announced Himself as the One the Báb had promised.
subjects.arc: Begin with the human transformation attributed to the teaching, approach the claims of station, and return through personal testimony to the life in which those claims are encountered.

order.why: Open with freedom from prejudice and the growth of unity and love.
Connect the teaching to the practical problem of war and antagonism.
shortened: Had the principles of unity, taught by the Christ, remained in the hearts, men would have refrained from war. Universalism must be retaught. Baha'u'llah has brought the force to unite the most antagonistic sects and bring all nations under one flag.

order.why: Read the sun image through its promised illumination of humanity.
Consider the language of a universal Educator and a luminous mirror.
Hear the identification with the promises of earlier scriptures.
shortened: Know thou verily, Baha'u'llah is the Promised One in all the Books and Tablets, and verily, this servant, is the herald of the Kingdom of God.

order.why: Keep distinct the stations of Bahá’u’lláh, the Báb, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá.
Encounter the reported view that the life itself is a standing miracle.
shortened: He answered 'He is the greatest of the world of humanity. He is peerless. He is beyond my limited Knowledge. I cannot describe him. Do you want any miracle? His very existence is a miracle; his walking is a miracle, his speaking is a miracle.
All his deeds, his words and his conducts are standing miracles.

order.why: Read the testimony to the force of His presence.
shortened: Then the Master added the Presence of the Blessed Perfection was awe-inspiring. Those who came into his Presence knelt down against their own will. They could not help themselves. They were awe-struck by the wonderful power and authority which emanated from Him.

order.why: Notice the visibility of joy and sadness in a remembered human encounter.
Hear Bahá’u’lláh’s own concise statement of His outward circumstances.
Explains the social purpose and gradual influence of Baha’u’llah’s Revelation through love and service to human needs.
Retain the family recollection about the place of origin of His parents.
Introduce the supplied statement of Abrahamic descent.
Keep the report of a gathering’s president distinct from direct self-description.
Read the more detailed supplied genealogical account.
Preserve the separately attributed explanation of that lineage.
shortened: Regarding the Blessed Beauty, He was not born of the line of Ishmael but was, rather, a descendant of one of the other brothers who had migrated to Persia and the Afghan territories. For, apart from Isaac and Ishmael, Abraham had six sons who all moved to Persia and to the Afghan regions.

order.why: Place the remembered affluence beside exile and confiscation.
shortened: When we were exiled from Persia our family was in a most sad condition, though formerly Baha'u'llah had enjoyed great affluence. By exiling us and confiscating all our estates the government hoped to blot out the family.

order.why: Retain the brief reported statement concerning spoken and written Arabic.
Approach the expansive revealed language of an incomparable Revelation.
shortened: These are days the like of which the eye of creation hath never seen, and in the like of which none of God's Messengers hath appeared save this most wondrous and incomparable Revelation. Through this Revelation is the decree of origination made manifest, were ye of them that are assured, and through this Revelation hath the power of God been established among His servants and His sovereignty manifested unto all possessed of keen insight and knowledge.

order.why: Return to the childhood capacities remembered by those around Him.
Read Shoghi Effendi’s portrayal of the majesty of the figure.
Close with the supplied framing of the period inspired by His life.

questions: How do the opening passages about overcoming prejudice shape the meaning of the later descriptions of majesty and power?
What can personal recollections disclose that a statement of spiritual station alone might leave unexplored?
How does distinguishing a revealed text, an interpretation, and a reported recollection affect the way this collection is read?
What might it mean to investigate a religious claim through the relation between teaching, conduct, and effects upon others?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the claim that signs of spiritual greatness are present from childhood.
Consider the mirror image and the continuing openness required by recognition.

references.label: 1 · John 10:37–38 — attending to the works
references.note: Jesus directs those who question Him to consider His works and what they disclose about His relationship with the Father. Compare that invitation with the collection’s testimony to words, conduct, and the power to unite. The comparison concerns an approach to recognition, while leaving the traditions’ distinct explanations of divine manifestation open to careful study.

subjects.displayTitle: Prophetic awareness: the light before its public dawning
subjects.introduction: Before Jesus was baptized, before any dove descended, the Word already was. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá insists on this: a Manifestation of God does not acquire His station at the hour of His public mission, as if an office were handed to Him, but is a Prophet from a beginning that has no beginning. Signs of greatness show in childhood; the learned are astonished by one who never sat in a school, because His light, like the sun’s, is not borrowed. Luke’s portrait of the boy in the temple, astonishing the teachers and yet growing in wisdom and stature, holds the same mystery in a single scene [1]. And yet Bahá’u’lláh can speak of being roused from sleep by the breeze of God, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá admits that the nature of such consciousness lies beyond us. To hold the image of awakening beside the fact of an innate station is to begin asking how the Manifestation’s preexistence, His special and untaught knowledge, and the divine will that moves Him belong to one reality.
subjects.arc: Begin with the enduring Word, approach the signs attributed to childhood, read the awakening images, and end by acknowledging the limit of what is known.

order.why: Open with the distinction between the Word’s station and the event of baptism.
shortened: In the Gospel it is said: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God." It follows then that Christ did not attain His Messianic station and His perfections at the moment of His baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in the form of a dove. Rather, the Word of God has always been, and will ever remain, in the loftiest heights of sanctity.

order.why: Read prophetic station in the language of an act of God beyond temporal limits.
Consider the argument from childhood signs to awareness of station.
shortened: From the beginning, that sanctified Reality is undoubtedly aware of the secret of existence, and from childhood the signs of greatness are clearly manifested in Him. How then could He fail, in spite of such bounties and perfections, to be conscious of His own station?

order.why: Recounts extraordinary knowledge and qualities from childhood despite the absence of formal schooling.

sourceQuestion.text: Question: On what date did the dawning of the Sun of Truth and the advent of the Blessed Beauty take place?

order.why: Hear the brief reported statement about Christ’s early knowledge of His mission. Keep the separately supplied report and its bracketed wording intact.
shortened: 'Abdu'l-Baha: "It was hidden from others, but manifest to him. The story about the dove is simply a metaphor. No dove came down. Amongst the people, John the Baptist felt that the Holy Spirit was in Christ. The Holy Spirit was always with Christ. He knew about his mission from early childhood."

order.why: Read the reported distinction between an inborn station and a conferred office.
shortened: The dignity and burden of prophethood is not conferred on the true Prophet, but it is inborn, created in Him.

order.why: Retain the description of birth signs within its particular source and station.
Approach the sun as an image of knowledge that does not borrow its light.
shortened: No one entered his presence without becoming awe-stricken by his might. The learned men who approached him were astounded at his knowledge, yet he never attended school nor learned of men. His friends and his family all testify to this, yet his teachings are the soul of this age.

The sun emanates from itself and does not draw its light from other sources. The divine teachers have the innate light; they have knowledge and understanding of all things in the universe; the rest of the world receives its light from them and through them the arts and sciences are revived in each age.

order.why: Preserve the concise criterion of innate rather than acquired knowledge.
shortened: Investigate the reality and in whomsoever these conditions are fulfilled, know ye of a certainty that he is the Great Master.
Thirdly: His Knowledge must be innate and spontaneous and not acquired.

order.why: Connect that criterion with the character of the writings.
shortened: But the light of this Perfect Man must be heavenly, not earthly; His perfections must be innate, not acquired; and His writings must be unbounded bestowals, not the products of the finite disciplines of this limited and contingent world.

order.why: Read the language that places even innate nature in relation to divine creation.
shortened: Say:  The Holy Spirit Itself hath been generated through the agency of a single letter revealed by this Most Great Spirit, if ye be of them that comprehend.  And that innate and untaught nature in its essence is called into being by the verses of God, the Help in Peril, the All-Glorious, the Best-Beloved.  Say:  This nature prideth itself in its relation to Our transcendent Truth, whilst We, for Our part, glory neither in it nor in aught else, for all beside Myself hath been created through the potency of My word, could ye but understand.

order.why: Encounter the image of a call awakening a sleeper.
Return to a personal childhood recollection of Bahá’u’lláh.
Distinguish being known by others from the knowledge attributed to the Manifestation.
A childhood recollection illustrating independent spiritual judgment before physical maturity.
Read the supplied provisional translation about awareness before manifestation.
Approach the symbolic School of God beyond ordinary chronology.
Hear awakening used in the language of prayer.
shortened: I lay asleep on the bed of self when lo, Thou didst waken me with the divine accents of Thy voice, and didst unveil to me Thy beauty, and didst enable me to listen to Thine utterances, and to recognize Thy Self, and to speak forth Thy praise, and to extol Thy virtues, and to be steadfast in Thy love.

order.why: Compare another provisional explanation of the lamp image.
Close with the explicit acknowledgment that the nature of this consciousness is unknown.

questions: How might an enduring spiritual station and a public moment of revelation be understood together?
What does the contrast between innate light and borrowed light clarify, and what does the image leave unexplained?
How can the language of awakening be read alongside statements of awareness from the beginning?
What intellectual or spiritual value lies in ending this collection with an acknowledgment of what we do not know?

neighbors.invitation: Read the awakening image alongside the supplied explanation that treats it as a metaphor.
Consider how knowledge is related to the needs and conditions of humanity.

references.label: 1 · Luke 2:46–52 — understanding, calling, and growth
references.note: Luke portrays the young Jesus listening, questioning, and astonishing His hearers, while His parents struggle to understand His words; the narrative also speaks of His growth in wisdom and stature. Compare the questions raised by this combination with the collection’s distinction between human appearance and an enduring spiritual station.

subjects.displayTitle: The reed and the breath: revelation and the divine will
subjects.introduction: A reed makes music only once it has been hollowed out, and even then the melody comes from the player, not the reed. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses that image for the Manifestation of God, whose heart is emptied of all but God and whose utterance comes from the divine Breath. Bahá’u’lláh describes His own calling in the same key: asleep on His couch when the breezes of the All-Glorious passed over Him, silent until He was made to speak, a leaf stirred by winds it cannot resist, straw before a great wind. The surrender is not withdrawal; it sends Him out into exile and prison to raise His voice between earth and heaven. Jesus saying that He seeks not His own will but the will of the One who sent Him [1] invites a close comparison, with due attention to how each tradition links the source of an utterance to its authority. For an ordinary believer the question becomes what freedom from self-seeking would change in how one speaks, decides and serves. The road leads on toward the Manifestation as mediator, toward the Primal Will and the Word, and toward servitude and submission to God.
subjects.arc: Begin with the reed’s music, follow the images of divine initiative, and move from the Manifestation’s mission toward the believer’s own work of consecration.

order.why: Hear that relationship expressed through the pen, tongue, and wind.
shortened: From my pen floweth only the summons which Thine own exalted pen hath voiced, and my tongue uttereth naught save what the Most Great Spirit hath itself proclaimed in the kingdom of Thine eternity. I am stirred by nothing else except the winds of Thy will, and breathe no word except the words which, by Thy leave and Thine inspiration, I am led to pronounce.

order.why: Open with a concrete image of speech arising through openness to another’s breath.
Consider the choice to make the divine purpose one’s purpose.
shortened: O Rida! The Wronged One makes mention of thee - He Who hath chosen for Himself no will or purpose, but hath chosen the will of the Intended One and the purpose of God, the Protector, the Self-Subsisting.

order.why: Read the general statement concerning the works of the Manifestations.
shortened: Be ye assured, moreover, that the works and acts of each and every one of these Manifestations of God, nay whatever pertaineth unto them, and whatsoever they may manifest in the future, are all ordained by God, and are a reflection of His Will and Purpose.

order.why: Follow the progression from silence and stillness to speech and action.
shortened: Say: By God! He was silent - God made Him speak. He was seated - the hands of power and might made Him arise. He was asleep - the breezes of the morn of Revelation that blew by God's will, the Lord of the Day of Return, awakened Him. Say: O people of the Bayan! He speaketh not of His own desire - to this testifieth that which hath been revealed from His Most Exalted Pen.

order.why: Attend to the response to those who blame the bearer of the call.
shortened: Say: O people! I was asleep when the Call awakened Me, and I was silent when the Truth, the Knower of the unseen, caused Me to speak and commanded Me to raise My voice in this atmosphere. This is not My crime, if ye be fair. Fear God, O people, and follow not the desires of every ignorant one, nor follow those who have denied the Witness and the Witnessed.

order.why: Compare the reported image of straw before a great wind.
Read the Báb’s testimony to acting by divine permission.
Let the theme enter the language of a personal supplication.
shortened: I beseech Thee by Thy Name through which the tribes have lamented, save those whom Thy pervading Will and Thy all-compelling Purpose have chosen, to grant me the Kawthar of Thy good-pleasure and to ordain for me what Thou hast ordained for Thy Messengers who spoke not except by Thy leave and command, and moved not except by Thy will.

order.why: Read the distinction between self-initiated appearance and divine manifestation. Preserve the supplied statement distinguishing revelation from impulse. Read the extended awakening passage with its supplied interpretive reference intact.
shortened: By God! He, the Glory of God (Baha), hath spoken not from mere impulse. He that hath given Him a voice is He that hath given a voice unto all things, that they may praise and glorify Him.
In the Tablet, addressed to His Majesty the Shah -- may God, blessed and glorified be He, assist him -- these words have streamed from the tongue of this Wronged One:

"O King! I was but a man like others, asleep upon My couch, when lo, the breezes of the All-Glorious were wafted over Me, and taught Me the knowledge of all that hath been. This thing is not from Me, but from One Who is Almighty and All-Knowing. And He bade Me lift up My voice between earth and heaven, and for this there befell Me what hath caused the tears of every man of understanding to flow.
Can anyone speak forth of his own accord that for which all men, both high and low, will protest against him?

order.why: Explicitly states that the Manifestation’s will is God’s will and that He speaks and moves only by divine command.
Encounter the emphatic denial that the Cause is under personal control.
Consider the explanation of rebukes outwardly addressed to Prophets.
shortened: Answer: Every divine utterance that takes the form of a rebuke, though it be outwardly addressed to the Prophets of God, is in reality directed to Their followers. The wisdom of this is naught but unalloyed mercy, that the people might not be dismayed, disheartened, or burdened by such reproaches and rebukes. These words are therefore outwardly addressed to the Prophets, but, even so, they are inwardly intended for the followers and not for the Messenger.

These holy Souls are like the leaves of a tree which are stirred into motion by the breeze and not of Their own accord, for They are attracted by the breaths of the love of God and have forsaken Their own will.

order.why: Return to the light and truth attributed to divine guidance.
Close with the consecration and cleansing of desire asked of the believer.
shortened: It behoveth thee to consecrate thyself to the Will of God. Whatsoever hath been revealed in His Tablets is but a reflection of His Will. So complete must be thy consecration, that every trace of worldly desire will be washed from thine heart. This is the meaning of true unity.

questions: What does the reed image suggest about the relationship between emptiness of self and fullness of expression?
How do the images of wind and awakening connect divine initiative with the Manifestation’s active mission?
What distinctions matter when comparing the Manifestation’s station with the believer’s effort to align life with a divine purpose?
How might freedom from self-seeking change the way a person speaks, decides, or serves?

neighbors.invitation: Keep the acknowledged limits of understanding prophetic consciousness in view.
Explore the connection between divine knowledge and the practical needs served by religion.

references.label: 1 · John 5:30 — the will of the One who sends
references.note: Jesus relates His judgment to hearing and to seeking the Father’s will rather than His own. Compare this formulation with the images of the reed and the wind. How do the passages connect the source of an utterance with its authority, and how do their different theological settings shape that connection?

subjects.displayTitle: Knowledge and revelation: insight in the service of humanity
subjects.introduction: Asked whether He was one who understood all mysteries and knew every science in detail, the Báb answered that He neither was nor is such a person. That refusal is the right place to start, because it unsettles the easy picture before the larger claims arrive: that the Manifestations of God know the realities underlying all created things and therefore found a religion fitted to humanity’s actual condition; that Bahá’u’lláh, who read no books of the learned, found whatever He wished to cite appearing before Him as on a tablet; that He was a man asleep on His couch when the breezes of the All-Glorious taught Him all that had been. Scholars in Persia brought Him the questions that baffled them and went away answered, a young man in a hat having expounded what twenty-five years of training could not. The point of such knowledge is always its purpose: a physician with a finger on the pulse of the world, foreseeing an illness without causing it. The Qur’án’s servant, given mercy and taught knowledge from God’s own presence, is a compact companion to these themes [1]. They lead on to the Holy Spirit, to the Manifestation as the recipient of revelation, and to the question of innate awareness.
subjects.arc: Begin with a statement that unsettles easy assumptions, consider knowledge through its purpose, and explore testimony, analogy, and the distinction between knowing and causing.

order.why: Place knowledge within the task of establishing a religion suited to human needs.
shortened: Briefly, the universal Manifestations of God are aware of the truths underlying the mysteries of all created things, and thus they found a religion that is based upon and consonant with the prevailing condition of humanity. For religion consists in the necessary relationships deriving from the realities of things. If the Manifestation of God--the divine Lawgiver--were not informed of the realities of things, if He did not understand the necessary relationships deriving from these realities, He would assuredly be incapable of establishing a religion consonant with the needs and conditions of the time.

order.why: Open with the Báb’s refusal of the description offered by a questioner.
shortened: Know that you seek one who is capable of understanding all mysteries and knowledgeable of all sciences in detail. God and His chosen ones bear witness that I neither was nor am such a one.

order.why: Consider foresight through the image of a physician reading signs.
shortened: The second kind of discovery is due to the fact that the Prophets are able Physicians and informed of the mysteries of the universe. They have Their finger on the pulse of the world, and They diagnose and foresee the ailments and illnesses which are to come. It is from the appearance, signs, and conditions of the universe itself that They infer these mysteries.

order.why: Hear Bahá’u’lláh’s account of access to the sayings and writings of others.
Read the knowledge received through the image of awakening.
Approach the testimony about answers given without religious schooling.
Encounter a particular remembered exchange with students and a scholar.
Read the wider account of questions and acknowledged answers.
Consider the open invitation to seekers of varied backgrounds.
shortened: All peoples, tribes, religions and paths were present in the Most Holy Court, and all were submissive and humble. Every seeker asked about the divine mysteries and received a healing, sufficient answer. And any person who asked about the most difficult questions of ancient arts and modern sciences, even obscure sciences, heard a convincing reply.

This matter is renowned throughout all regions and known to all in every direction, despite everyone knowing that throughout His life He had neither studied nor been taught. What greater miracle than this?

order.why: Return to innate light and the renewal of arts and sciences.
shortened: The divine teachers have the innate light; they have knowledge and understanding of all things in the universe; the rest of the world receives its light from them and through them the arts and sciences are revived in each age.

order.why: Distinguish sharing a landscape from perceiving a divine call.
shortened: Many people crossed the desert of Sinai but it was Moses who heard the voice of God because the divine Manifestations have a spiritual power peculiar to themselves.

order.why: Compare the reported contrast between prophetic sight and ordinary discovery.
Retain the supplied explanatory parenthesis about intuition and disciples.
shortened: (That is, the Prophets prove the existence of Intuition or Inner Reason, by showing forth themselves such a comprehension which is beyond the power of any man. They also inspire their disciples with, and develop in them, the same power. This is illustrated in the life, prophetic vision and deeds of the Prophets and their true followers.)

order.why: Hear the reported description of the Manifestation’s explanations as revelation.
Consider the distinction between corporeal and heavenly station.
shortened: All these things refer to the corporeal station of the Manifestations; but their heavenly station encompasses all things, is aware of all mysteries, is informed of all signs, and rules supreme over all things. And this is equally true both before and after the intimation of their mission. That is why Christ said: "I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last"--that is, there has never been, nor shall there ever be, any change or alteration in Me.

order.why: Read the statement about knowledge beyond past and future.
Follow the reported enumeration through the end of its complete source sentence.
Keep the remembered account concerning the Most Great Branch in its own attribution.
Distinguishes the essential knowledge of the Manifestations from knowledge bestowed on their followers.
Read the reported reply concerning knowledge when it is needed.
Approach the abundance of imagery used for a reality beyond ready comprehension.
shortened: There is treasured within this Youth a melody which, were even less than a needle's eye thereof to be disclosed, would cause the mountains to crumble, the leaves to wither, the fruits to fall from the trees, faces to bow down, and all countenances to turn toward this King Whom thou beholdest in the form of fire clothed in light, and at times thou seest Him as waves in this surging ocean, and at times thou beholdest Him as the Tree whose roots are firmly fixed in the earth of grandeur and whose branches and twigs have reached unto a station that hath transcended the Mighty Throne, and at times thou findest Him in the form of the Beloved in this Raiment which none among all creation can recognize, and were they to desire to know Him, they would swoon in their spirits, save him who cometh unto his Lord with a sound heart.

order.why: Retain the supplied criterion of answering humanity’s difficult questions.
shortened: Fourthly: He must answer the questions of all the sages, solve all the difficult problems of humanity and be able to withstand all the persecutions and sufferings heaped upon him.
Sixthly: His Knowledge must be infinite and his wisdom all-comprehensive.

order.why: Keep the recollection of physical capacities distinct from claims about revelation.
End with the clear distinction between foreseeing an event and causing it.
shortened: As to the pronouncements which, through divine revelation, have issued from the Prophets regarding the advent of the Promised One of the Torah, these likewise were not the cause of Christ's appearance. But the hidden mysteries of the days to come were revealed to the Prophets, who thus became acquainted with future events and who proclaimed them in turn. This knowledge and proclamation were not the cause of the occurrence of these events.

questions: How does the opening denial affect the questions you bring to the later affirmations of knowledge?
What connection do these readings make between understanding reality and responding to humanity’s needs?
How do the images of a physician, an inward eye, and a visible tablet illuminate different aspects of knowing?
Why might the distinction between foreknowledge and causation matter for understanding prophecy and human responsibility?

neighbors.invitation: Compare the affirmations here with the stated limit on knowing the nature of prophetic consciousness.
Consider the reed image as an account of the source of a revealed utterance.

references.label: 1 · Qur’án 18:65 — mercy and knowledge bestowed by God
references.note: The verse introduces a servant through mercy received and knowledge taught by God. Compare this pairing with the compilation’s treatment of knowledge as serving the needs and conditions of humanity. The connection invites inquiry into the relation between insight and its purpose without assigning identical stations to the figures being described.

subjects.displayTitle: Religions of the East: love, recognition, and careful comparison
subjects.introduction: Asked for his message, a Buddhist told ‘Abdu’l-Bahá simply: love. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá pressed him, because love is not yet a message until it becomes something a person can do with their attention, their restraint and their hands. That exchange sets the tone for an encounter with the religions of the East. He teaches that Krishna and Buddha taught the one God, that the tree Buddha planted grew from a sapling to shade all Asia, that the Hindu who attains Nirvana and the Christian who finds salvation are naming a single nearness, and that a teacher should begin with the truths already treasured in another’s faith. He also voices sharp criticisms, and his reported words describe Buddha in differing ways, so the traditions deserve to be heard in their own voices alongside him. The Mettā Sutta’s practice of boundless care for all beings and the Bhagavad Gītā’s portrait of the compassionate devotee of Krishna speak here in their own terms [1] [2]. From this meeting the path opens onto oneness and the unity of religion, onto progressive revelation, and onto the renewal that every faith has needed in its turn.
subjects.arc: Begin with love and the question of how to practice it, attend to encounters and spiritual kinship, then read the difficult judgments with primary voices from the traditions in view.

order.why: Affirms the shared spiritual aim of Buddha, Zoroaster, Christ and the other Prophets.
Hear the counsel to begin with truths meaningful within another person’s religion.
Immediately ask how an apparently universal word becomes a practical message.
shortened: I met a man this morning who belongs to the sect of Buddhists and I said to him, "What is your message?" He replied "l'Amour, Love!" I said, "Yes, but what besides that?" He repeated, "Love, that is all, that is the only message."
But the word Love is not a message; the word Love indicates an infinite thing, and how shall we bring an infinite thing into relation with humanity which is finite?

order.why: Consider the reported story of patience in the face of hostility.
shortened: When Buddha sent His disciples to teach, He asked them: "If you go to a city and they deny you, what will you do?" They said: "We will pray and be thankful for they do not beat us." He asked: "If they beat you, what will you do?" They replied: "We will still be grateful for they do not imprison us." He asked: "If they imprison you?" They said: "We will still be thankful because they do not kill us." He asked: "If they kill you?" They replied: "Then we will be even more thankful for we will have attained the supreme martyrdom in the path of God."

order.why: Pause over the tree image for the spread of a teaching.
Read the claim of a common spirit and purpose among the Manifestations.
Compare the religious vocabularies used in a reported conversation.
Approach the question of symbolic religious expectation.
Read the invitation to turn attention toward the present work of peace.
shortened: Now is not the time for us to discuss the station and ranks of those who have gone before. We must look to the present. Whatever is past is past. Now is the time to confine our words to the Most Great Luminary of peace and tranquility of this age. We must speak of the Blessed Beauty and give news of His counsels, exhortations and teachings.

order.why: Retain the reported comparison of the settings in which teachers appeared.
shortened: When Christ appeared, the people among whom he came were in a low state of intelligence there was little or no discussion of abstruse questions among them. Buddha, though earlier, came to a part of the world where civilisation was much more advanced, which was ripe in philosophical and metaphysical speculations. Mahomet found wild tribes and hordes of uncivilised barbarians.

order.why: Encounter the account of Buddha and Confucius in Some Answered Questions.
Read the separately reported claim concerning monotheism.
shortened: Brahma, Krishna and Buddha never taught polytheism. They were the Supreme teachers of monotheism like all the other prophets of God; but the succeeding generations misconstrued their words and in order to further their own selfish interests they fabricated these false doctrines.

order.why: Preserve a differing reported description of Buddha and a criticism of reincarnation.
Consider the aging image used for a religious tradition.
Keep the historical report’s broad characterizations visibly within its attribution.
Read the reported criticism of the use of images.
shortened: The attributes of Divinity are assigned to the idols of India and today the likeness of Buddha is worshipped by several hundred millions of human souls.

order.why: Compare the concern about imagined physical portrayals of religious founders.
Retain the account of arguments about the sun as a distinct reported conversation.
Keep the supplied classification of Confucius beside the earlier differing accounts.
Turn to the challenge made to prejudice against Buddhists.
End with the possibility of former antagonists associating in love.
Open with the message of love attributed to Krishna.

questions: What changes when love is treated as a practice involving attention, restraint, and action rather than only as an agreeable word?
How might the Buddhist and Hindu primary readings deepen or complicate the broad descriptions in this collection?
What is needed to compare spiritual terms across traditions without assuming that they mean exactly the same thing?
How can a conviction about religious unity increase curiosity about another tradition’s own understanding of itself?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the release from inherited prejudice as part of the teaching’s stated purpose.
Explore the relation between a religious teaching and the human conditions it addresses.

references.label: 1 · Karaṇīya Mettā Sutta (Sn 1.8) — a practice of boundless care
references.note: In the Amaravati Sangha’s translation, goodwill extends to living beings near and far and is sustained in ordinary postures and activities. Compare that practical cultivation with the question of how love becomes a message for human life. Let this Buddhist teaching speak in its own terms alongside the collection’s descriptions of Buddhism.

references.label: 2 · Bhagavad Gītā 12:13–14 — compassion and devotion
references.note: These verses describe the dear devotee through friendliness, compassion, freedom from possessiveness, steadiness, and dedication of mind and understanding to Krishna. Read the verses in this Bhaktivedanta translation alongside the account of Krishna’s message of love. What ethical affinities appear, and what distinct understanding of devotion remains essential to the passage?
